newsitem.title: USA: NHL ICE HOCKEY-LEMIEUX LEAVES GAME AT THE TOP.
newsitem.headline: NHL ICE HOCKEY-LEMIEUX LEAVES GAME AT THE TOP.

text.p: Few athletes in history have walked away while still at the top of their sport, but at 31 and on the heels of his sixth National Hockey League scoring title Mario Lemieux has left the ice.
Lemeiux's sensational career with the Pittsburgh Penguins ended Saturday, but not before the standard for claiming the mantle of superstar had been raised a few notches.

"Not being able to play the way I once played is very frustrating," Lemieux said, explaining one of his reasons for retiring. Of course, Lemieux only pales in comparison to himself -- hardly a fair standard for anyone to measure up to.
His career began in a way that only Hollywood sreenwriters could have dreamed up.

Lemieux, whose name appropriately means "the best", stepped onto NHL ice 13 years ago at Boston Garden and on his first shift, with his first shot, scored a goal. The legacy of Le Magnifique had begun.

The NHL's top draft pick at 18, Lemieux came to the league's worst team in 1984 and almost single-handedly kept it in existance. "He saved the Pittsburgh franchise and lifted it to two Stanley Cups," said Mark Messier, a star on six Cup-winning teams.

He leaves behind statistics stunning as his stick handling and a plethora of awards, including Rookie of the Year, six NHL scoring titles, three Most Valuable Player awards, twice MVP of the playoffs.
Lemieux's goals per game average of .823 is the greatest in NHL history -- better even than Wayne Gretzky, who owns every other offensive mark in the record books.

"When I was growing up in Czechoslovakia, there were only two players I ever wanted to play with, Mario Lemieux and Wayne Gretzky. I was very lucky. I got to play with the greatest player in hockey," said Penguins star Jaromir Jagr.
"I don't care what anybody says about anyone else, there is no way a guy can be more talented than this guy," Flyers goalie Ron Hextall said of Lemieux. "It's humanly impossible."
But Lemieux, all 6'4" (1.93 m), 220 pounds (100 kg) of him, is tired.

Not of the nightly heroics or adoration, but of what has become of the game he's loved since first skating on frozen ponds outside Montreal, of the clutching and grabbing by less talented players -- "the NHL could be the most popular sport in the world if the stars were able to show our true skills" -- and of wondering how long his health would hold out.

Of the eight pages he takes up in the Penguins' media guide, a full page is devoted to injuries and illnesses, accounting for more than 200 games missed, not to mention the ones he played with such severe back pain that others had to tie his skates for him.
"If Mario Lemieux had stayed healthy, he would have broken all of my records for goals, assists and points," Gretzky said.
Lemieux twice needed back surgery -- perhaps the result of carrying his team on it for so many years -- and suffered from Hodgkin's disease, a form of cancer that only slowed him down.

In one of the most inspirational feats of an awe-inpsiring career, Lemieux returned after taking off the entire 1994-95 season to recover from back surgery and the effects of radiation treatments to win his fifth scoring title.
This season he took over sixth place on the NHL all-time goals list (613) and again led the league with 122 points -- the 10th time he reached at least 100 points for a season.
"He just does things that none of us can do. Certainly, I can't," said Mike Gartner, himself a future Hall of Famer.

Lemieux became a Canadian national hero in 1987 when he scored 11 goals in the Canada Cup tournament, including the winning goal in the final against the Soviet Union. Gretzky and Messier have each sited playing that tournament alongside Lemieux among their fondest hockey memories.
Lemieux enjoyed his most prolific season in 1988-89 when he piled up 199 points with 85 goals. Five of those came on New Year's Eve in what Lemieux considers his finest game.

That night against New Jersey, Lemieux became the only NHL player ever to score five different ways in one game -- at even strength, short-handed, on a power play, on a penalty shot and into an empty net.
In 1990-91, Lemieux played just 26 regular-season games due to back surgery and still carried the Pens to the first of their consecutive Stanley Cup championships.

In 1992-93, Lemieux was diognosed with Hodgkin's and missed 20 games. The night of his final strength-sapping radiation treatment, he not only played, but scored a goal. Penguins owner Howard Baldwin said Lemieux "transcends sports. What he has overcome ... you will never see that again."
Paul Coffey, who owns most NHL scoring records by a defenceman, has counted among his teammates, Lemieux, Gretzky, Messier, Steve Yzerman, Sergei Fedorov and now Eric Lindros.
"I've been fortunate enough to have played with a lot of great players," Coffey said, "and Mario is by far the most talented."

And yet Lemieux's ego seemed to exist in reverse proportion to his immense talents. He is shy, humble and understated and has shied away from marketing himself in the manner so prevalent with stars and would-be stars of the day.
"Mario brought a quiet dignity with him each and every day," former Penguin Troy Loney wrote in his hockey column.
Lemieux endured deafening, emotional ovations as his final season wound down, especially in hockey-mad Montreal, where he was moved to tears by the reception.
In Boston, Bruins' captain Ray Bourque, from whom Lemieux stole the puck before scoring his first NHL goal, presented Lemieux with an inscribed seat from the old Boston Garden.

Even in Philadephia, where the rival Penguins are hated, Lemieux skated one last time around the rink to a thunderous standing ovation after Pittsburgh was eliminated from the playoffs Saturday, bringing the Lemieux era to an end.

"I think, looking back, I've pretty much done it all," Lemieux said. "Just the idea that I brought a winning tradition to Pittsburgh, that was the most important thing. Having done that, I can go out in peace.
"Everything's quite all right with me."
